Commentarii in epistulam ad Romanos (I.1-XII.21) (in catenis)
i1
ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ. Τρίτον ἔστιν ἰδεῖν τὸ ἀφωρισμένος εἰς
εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ· καὶ ἐν τῇ πρὸς Γαλάτας ὁ ἀπόστολος περὶ ἑαυτοῦ τοιαῦτά φησιν·
ὅτε δὲ εὐδόκη εν ὁ θεό , ὁ ἀφορί α με ἐκ κοιλία μητρό μου, ἀποκαλύψαι τὸν υἱὸν
αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐμοί. ἐπιλαμβάνονται δὲ τῶν τοιούτων λέξεων οἱ μὴ συνιέντες τὸν ἐκ
προγνώσεως θεοῦ προωρισμένον αἴτιον τυγχάνοντα τοῦ γίνεσθαι τὰ
προγινωσκόμενα· καὶ οἴονται διὰ τούτων εἰσάγειν τοὺς ἐκ κατασκευῆς καὶ φύσεως
σωζομένους. τινὲς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων ἀναιροῦσι ῥητῶν,
συγχρώμενοι καὶ τῷ ἀπηλλοτριώθη αν οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπὸ μήτρα ἐν ψαλμοῖς
εἰρημένῳ. πρὸς μὲν οὖν τοῦτο εὐχερῶς ἔστιν ἀπαντῆσαι, ἐρωτῶντας περὶ τῆς ἑξῆς
λέξεως· γέγραπται γὰρ ἀπηλλοτριώθη αν οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπὸ μήτρα , ἐπλανήθη αν
ἀπὸ γα τρό , ἐλάλη αν ψευδῆ· θυμὸ αὐτοῖ κατὰ τὴν ὁμοίω ιν τοῦ ὄφεω . καὶ
πευσόμεθά γε τῶν ὡς σαφεῖ τῇ λέξει ἐπιβαινόντων, εἰ οἱ ἀπαλλοτριωθέντες
ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπὸ μήτρας ἅμα τῷ ἐξελθεῖν ἀπὸ γαστρὸς τῆς μητρὸς αὐτῶν
ἐπλανήθησαν καὶ τῆς σωζούσης ὁδοῦ ἐσφάλησαν, αὐτοὶ εἰς τοῦτο ἐνεργήσαντες. πῶς
δὲ οἱ ἀπαλλοτριωθέντες ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπὸ μήτρας ἀπὸ γαστρὸς ἐπλανήθησάν τε καὶ
ἐλάλησαν ψευδῆ; οὐ γὰρ δὴ δείξουσιν ὅτι ἅμα τῷ γεννηθῆναι ἔναρθρον φωνὴν
προήκαντο, ψευδῆ τινὰ προφερόμενοι. ἀλλ' εἰ προσέχομεν τοῖς προτεταγμένοις τοῦ
προορισμοῦ ἐν τῇ ἐξεταζομένῃ ἐπιστολῇ λεγομένοις, δυνησόμεθα, τὰ περι σπῶντα
τοὺς ἁπλουστέρους πρὸς παραδοχὴν τοῦ ἀδικίαν κατηγοροῦντος κατὰ τοῦ θείου
δόγματος καθελόντες, ἀπολογήσασθαι περὶ τοῦ ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς ἀφορίζοντος καὶ
εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ ἀφορίζοντος τὸν δοῦλον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ κλητὸν ἀπόστολον
Παῦλον. οὕτω δὲ ἔχει τὰ ῥητά· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ι τὸν θεὸν πάντα υνεργεῖ
εἰ ἀγαθόν, τοῖ κατὰ πρόθε ιν κλητοῖ οὖ ιν· ὅτι οὓ προέγνω, καὶ προώρι εν
υμμόρφου τῆ εἰκόνο τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, εἰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν πρωτότοκον ἐν πολλοῖ
ἀδελφοῖ · οὓ δὲ προώρι εν, τούτου καὶ ἐκάλε εν· καὶ οὓ ἐκάλε εν, τούτου καὶ
ἐδικαίω εν· οὓ δὲ ἐδικαίω εν, τούτου καὶ ἐδόξα εν. πρόσχωμεν οὖν τῇ τάξει τῶν
λεγομένων. δικαιοῖ ὁ θεὸς καλέσας πρότερον, οὐκ ἂν δικαιώσας οὓς μὴ ἐκάλεσεν·
καλεῖ δὲ πρὸ τῆς κλήσεως προορίσας, οὐκ ἂν καλέσας οὓς μὴ προώρισεν· καὶ ἔστιν
αὐτῷ ἀρχὴ τῆς κλήσεως καὶ τῆς δικαιώσεως οὐχ ὁ προορισμός· οὗτος γὰρ εἰ ἦν ἀρχὴ
τῶν ἑξῆς, κἂν πιθανώτατα ἐκράτουν οἱ παρεισάγοντες τὸν περὶ φύσεως ἄτοπον
λόγον· ἀνωτέρω δέ ἐστι τοῦ προορισμοῦ ἡ πρόγνωσις· οὓ γὰρ προέγνω, φησί, καὶ
προώρι εν υμμόρφου τῆ εἰκόνο τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ. προενατενίσας οὖν ὁ θεὸς τῷ
εἱρμῷ τῶν ἐσομένων, καὶ κατανοήσας ῥοπὴν τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν τῶνδέ τινων ἐπὶ εὐσέ
βειαν καὶ ὁρμὴν ἐπὶ ταύτην μετὰ τὴν ῥοπήν, καὶ ὡς ὅλοι ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδώσουσι τῷ
κατ' ἀρετὴν ζῇν, προέγνω αὐτούς, γινώσκων μὲν τὰ ἐνιστάμενα προγινώσκων δὲ τὰ
μέλλοντα· καὶ οὓς οὕτω προέγνω, προώρισεν συμμόρφους ἐσομένους τῆς εἰκόνος
τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ. ἔστιν οὖν τις ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, εἰκὼν τυγχάνων τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ
ἀοράτου, καὶ τούτου εἰκὼν ἡ λεγομένη εἰκὼν τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ· ἥντινα νομίζομεν
εἶναι ἣν ἀνέλαβεν ψυχὴν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνθρωπίνην, γενομένην διὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν
τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ θεοῦ εἰκόνα. ταύτης δέ, ἣν οἰόμεθα εἰκόνος εἰκόνα εἶναι [τοῦ υἱοῦ]
τοῦ θεοῦ, συμμόρφους προώρισεν γενέσθαι ὁ θεός, οὓς διὰ τὴν περὶ αὐτῶν
πρόγνωσιν προώρισεν. οὐ γομιστέον τοίνυν εἶναι τῶν ἐσομένων αἰτίαν τὴν
πρόγνωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ· ἀλλ' ἐπεὶ ἔμελλεν γίνεσθαι κατ' ἰδίας ὁρμὰς τοῦ ποιοῦντος, διὰ
τοῦτο προέγνω, εἰδὼς τὰ πάντα πρὸ γενέσεως αὐτῶν· καὶ ὡς εἰδὼς τὰ πάντα πρὸ
γενέσεως αὐτῶν τούσδε μέν τινας προέγνω καὶ προώρισεν συμμόρφους ἐσομένους
τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ἄλλους δὲ εἶδεν ἀπηλλοτριωμένους. ἐὰν δέ τις
pass_a_gloss: Paul, set apart for the gospel of God, says in Galatians that when God was pleased, He set him apart from his mother's womb to reveal His Son in him. Those who do not understand God's foreknowledge and predestination misinterpret such words, thinking they bring in those preserved by nature and constitution, while some even deny what is in our power from these statements, using the psalm where sinners are alienated from the womb. But this is easily answered by asking about the following words: it is written that sinners are alienated from the womb, they have gone astray from birth, they have spoken lies; their anger is according to the likeness of the serpent. We will question those who take the words plainly: if those alienated sinners from the womb, upon coming out of their mother's womb, had wandered and strayed from the saving way by their own doing, how could they have wandered and spoken falsely? For they could not have uttered a joint infant voice speaking falsehoods at birth. But if we attend to the things said beforehand about predestination in the letter under examination, we can, by removing those who lead the simple to consent to accusing injustice against the divine doctrine, defend the fact that God sets apart from the womb and sets apart for the gospel of God the servant Jesus Christ, called apostle Paul. Thus it stands: we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those called according to purpose; whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers; and whom He predestined, He also called; and whom He called, He also justified; and whom He justified, He also glorified. Therefore, let us proceed in order of the things said: God justifies having called beforehand; He would not have justified those He did not call; and He calls having predestined beforehand; He would not have called those He did not predestine; and it is to Him the beginning of the call and justification, not predestination. For if predestination were the beginning of the following, those bringing in the anomalous argument of nature would most easily prevail. But above predestination is foreknowledge: for whom He foreknew, He says, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son. God, having beforehand attended to the order of the coming things, and having considered the inclination of these things from us toward security and impulse after that inclination, and as they will give themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them, knowing the present things and foreknowing the future things; and whom He so foreknew, He predestined to be conformed sons of the image of His Son. Therefore there is the Son of God, who is the image of the invisible God, and this is the image spoken of, the image of the Son of God, which we believe to be the soul the Son of God took, human, made through the virtue of God's image into an image. And this, which we think to be an image of an image [of the Son] of God, God has predestined to become conformed through His foreknowledge concerning them; but we must not think that the foreknowledge of God is the cause of the future things. Rather, since He was about to act according to His own impulse, He foreknew, knowing all things before their generation; and as knowing all things before their generation, He foreknew and predestined some to be conformed sons of the image of His Son, and saw others as alienated.
pass_b_english: Paul, chosen for the gospel of God, affirms in his letter to the Galatians that when God found it pleasing, He set him apart from his mother’s womb to reveal His Son within him. Those who misunderstand God’s foreknowledge and predestination twist these words, supposing they point only to those preserved by nature and constitution, while others even deny what rests within our power, citing the psalm that declares sinners alienated from the womb. Yet this is readily answered by examining the words that follow: it is written that sinners are estranged from the womb, they have strayed from birth, they have uttered lies; their fury bears the likeness of the serpent. We must challenge those who take these words literally: if those sinners, alienated from the womb, had immediately wandered from the path of salvation and spoken falsehood upon birth by their own accord, how could they have done so? For they could not have formed a coherent infant voice to speak lies at the moment of delivery. But if we reflect on what was said earlier in this very letter about predestination, we can, by setting aside those who mislead the simple into accusing God of injustice, uphold the truth that God both sets apart from the womb and sets apart for the gospel of God the servant Jesus Christ, known as the apostle Paul. Thus it stands: we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those called according to purpose; whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers; and whom He predestined, He also called; and whom He called, He also justified; and whom He justified, He also glorified. Therefore, let us follow the sequence of what has been said: God justifies because He called beforehand; He would not justify those He did not call; and He calls because He predestined beforehand; He would not call those He did not predestine; and it is to Him that the beginning of the call and justification belongs, not predestination. For if predestination were the starting point of what follows, those who advance the strange argument of nature would easily prevail. But above predestination lies foreknowledge: for whom He foreknew, He declares, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son. God, having beforehand attended to the order of coming things, and having considered the inclination of these things in us toward security and impulse after that inclination, and as they will surrender themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them, knowing the present and foreknowing the future; and whom He so foreknew, He predestined to be conformed as sons in the image of His Son. Therefore there is the Son of God, who is the image of the invisible God, and this is the image spoken of—the image of the Son of God—which we believe to be the soul the Son of God assumed, human, formed through the virtue of God’s image into an image. And this, which we regard as an image of an image [of the Son] of God, God has predestined to become conformed through His foreknowledge concerning them; yet we must not suppose that God’s foreknowledge is the cause of future things. Rather, since He was about to act according to His own impulse, He foreknew, knowing all things before their generation; and as knowing all things before their generation, He foreknew and predestined some to be conformed as sons in the image of His Son, and saw others as alienated.

We must not confuse the order of divine action: it is not that God first predestines and then calls, but that His foreknowledge precedes and undergirds both. The psalm’s words about sinners alienated from the womb are not to be read as a denial of human responsibility, but as a description of a condition that, from birth, inclines toward falsehood—yet even then, the capacity for choice remains, however dim. To imagine that infants could speak lies in unison at birth is to misunderstand both language and moral agency. But when we read Paul’s own words in Galatians, we see that his separation from the womb was not a mere natural endowment, but a divine act aimed at revealing Christ in him—thus grounding the apostolic calling in God’s purpose, not human merit. This is why we affirm that all things work together for good for those who love God, not because they earned it, but because they were called according to His eternal purpose. The chain is clear: foreknowledge leads to predestination, predestination to calling, calling to justification, justification to glorification—each step dependent on the prior, none originating in predestination alone. If we reverse this order and make predestination the first cause, we open the door to those who would blame God for injustice, as if He arbitrarily chose some and rejected others. But Scripture refuses such a reading: God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of what comes to be, but the reflection of His knowledge of what will be, grounded in His eternal understanding of hearts inclined toward virtue or alienation. Thus, He foreknew some as those who would yield to virtue, others as those who would remain alienated—not because He made them so, but because He saw what they would become, in freedom, before time began.

choices.issue: Whether the psalm’s description of sinners alienated from the womb implies innate moral incapacity from birth.
choices.choice: The psalm describes a condition present from birth, but does not negate the capacity for choice; infants cannot speak lies in unison, proving moral agency requires development, yet the inclination toward falsehood is real even early on.

choices.issue: Whether God’s foreknowledge is the cause of future events or merely His knowledge of them.
choices.choice: God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of future things, but His knowledge of them, grounded in His eternal understanding of inclinations—He foreknew because He was about to act according to His own impulse, not because His foreknowledge caused the act.
